# Loch Lomond & The Trossachs National Park

Scroll down


## Scotland’s first National Park

**A place where the lowlands and highlands meet, with varied scenery of rolling lowland landscapes, tranquil lochsand rugged mountains in the north.**

These landscapes create a diverse range of habitats for a variety of wildlife including red squirrels, black grouse, golden eagles, osprey, pine marten and otters. The National Park Authority works to inspire communities, visitors and partners to enhance and protect this special place.

- [@lomondtrossachs](https://twitter.com/@lomondtrossachs)
- [lomondtrossachs](https://facebook.com/lomondtrossachs)
- [lomondtrossachs](https://instagram.com/lomondtrossachs)

[lochlomond-trossachs.org](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/)

## Go explore

Just a stone’s throw away from Scotland’s central belt, there’s something for everyone to enjoy, whether you fancy a peaceful stroll along a loch shore or a wild outdoor adventure.

[![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/Key_activity_walking-600x400.jpg)\\
\\
Activity](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/things-to-do/walking/admire-autumn-from-these-top-trails/)

### [Walking , Activity](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/things-to-do/walking/admire-autumn-from-these-top-trails/)

Expect dramatic scenery in the Autumn months as the leaves start to turn. Admire the view from these top trails.

[![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/Key_activity_cycling-600x400.jpg)\\
\\
Activity](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/things-to-do/cycling/)

### [Cycling , Activity](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/things-to-do/cycling/)

There are lots of different cycling routes available in the National Park for all abilities, including family-friendly bike rides and hardcore mountain trails.

[![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/Key_activity_wildlife_watching-600x400.jpg)\\
\\
Activity](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/things-to-see/wildlife-nature/)

### [Watching wildlife , Activity](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/things-to-see/wildlife-nature/)

The National Park is brimming with wildlife. You could encounter a red squirrel in the forest or golden eagles soaring high above. You might even catch a glimpse of an otter hunting along the loch shores.

![Special qualities](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/Special_qualities_pucks_glen-1600x1080.jpg)

## What makes it special?

Loch Lomond & The Trossachs National Park is celebrated for the scenic quality of its landscapes and highly valued for its rich natural and cultural heritage.

Here are a few things that make the National Park special:

Its special landscapes include lochs, coastlines, forests and striking contrasts where the lowlands and highlands meet.

It’s a working landscape, which has been influenced through generations by the people who live and work there.

It’s steeped in history and heritage, with ruined castles, charming towns and villages, archaeological discoveries and scenery admired by famous poets in times gone by.

Six of Scotland’s Great Trails (long distance routes) connect in and around the National Park and are part of the national walking network across Scotland.

Its close proximity to urban areas allows visitors the opportunity to learn and connect with nature on their doorstep.

## Did you know?

There are 21 Munros (mountains above 3,000ft) in the National Park and the highest is Ben More at 1,174m.

# A place of contrasts

Located only an hour’s drive away for 50% of Scotland’s population, Loch Lomond & The Trossachs National Park is a popular visitor destination offering a wide variety of activities for everyone to enjoy.

You could visit a charming local village and learn about the area’s heritage, take a leisurely stroll along a tranquil loch or bag a mighty Munro.

It’s a treasure trove of discovery and a fantastic place to reconnect with the great outdoors.

![Conic Hill over looking Loch Lomond, Highland Boundary Fault line](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/Middle_block_Conic_Hill-1800x1080.jpg)
Conic Hill over looking Loch Lomond, Highland Boundary Fault line

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/Getting_Around_transport-580x580.jpg)

### Getting around

Loch Lomond & The Trossachs National Park is easily accessible from Scotland’s central belt. There are lots of [public transport](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/plan-your-visit/getting-to-the-park/) networks in and around the National Park and there are also great [cycle routes](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/things-to-do/cycling/) for active travel. Why not leave the car at home and make your journey here part of the holiday?

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/Getting_Around_Responsible-580x580.jpg)

### Visit responsibly

You can help to look after this special place by thinking about how you can be a responsible visitor when planning your trip. Loch Lomond & The Trossachs National Park Authority has some [useful information](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/looking-after-the-park/be-a-responsible-visitor/) on reducing waste, camping responsibly and even what to do when you need to poo in the great outdoors!

![](https://nationalparks.uk/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/Getting_Around_camping-580x580.jpg)

### Camping in the National Park

Loch Lomond & The Trossachs National Park has [seasonal byelaws](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/things-to-do/camping/) between the months of March and September, which mean that you may need a permit or to stay at a campsite in some areas. Please read the guidance before planning your camping trip.

# Getting to the Park

Loch Lomond & The Trossachs National Park is easily accessible by all means of transport. We would love it if you could come to the National Park by public transport. Why not make your journey here part of your holiday and take in the views rather than focusing on the car in front?

Like all the national parks in the UK, entry to Loch Lomond & The Trossachs National Park is free.

### National Park Journey Planner

![journey-planner-download](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/Journey_planner_930x310px-930x310-c-default.jpg)

Download our Journey Planner

The easiest way to see all travel options available in one place is by using the [National Park Journey Planner](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/plan-your-visit/national-park-journey-planner/) (available online or as an iOS/Google Play app). This tool makes it easier to research, plan and book your day trip. You can even compare the carbon emissions of different transport modes too.

#### Plan your visit

Start planning your journey below, or download the app on:

- [Google Play](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=ltd.ember.lochlomond)
- [App Store](https://apps.apple.com/gb/app/national-park-journey-planner/id1567048974)

### By train

![scotrail-train-stationed-in-balloch-station-with-tullie-inn-building-white-and-orange-behind](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/04/Balloch-Train-banner-930x310-c-default.jpg)

Visit by train

There are two key train lines that provide access to the National Park.

- **Glasgow – [Balloch](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/discover-the-park/towns-villages/balloch/)**: ScotRail operate a [direct line from Glasgow Queen Street](https://www.scotrail.co.uk/scotland-by-rail/destinations/enjoy-loch-lomond-by-train) and the journeys takes ~50 minutes and run approximately every 30min; from the station it is a short walk to catch a cruise on the loch or wander through Balloch Castle Park
- **Glasgow – Oban/Fort William**: ScotRail’s [West Highlands Line](https://www.scotrail.co.uk/scotland-by-rail/great-scenic-rail-journeys/west-highland-line-glasgow-oban-and-fort-williammallaig) is considered one of the most scenic in the country and provides stops in and close to the National Park (Helensburgh, Garelochhead, [Arrochar](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/discover-the-park/towns-villages/arrochar/) & [Tarbet](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/discover-the-park/towns-villages/tarbet/), Ardlui, [Crianlarich](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/discover-the-park/towns-villages/crianlarich/) and [Tyndrum](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/discover-the-park/towns-villages/tyndrum/)); jump off at [Tarbet](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/discover-the-park/towns-villages/tarbet/) and Ardlui to connect with [Waterbus services](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/things-to-do/water-activities/waterbus/) across to [Loch Lomond](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/things-to-see/lochs-in-the-national-park/loch-lomond/)’s eastern shores and the [West Highland Way](http://westhighlandway.org/), [Ben Lomond](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/things-to-do/walking/hillwalking/ben-lomond/) and [Balmaha](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/discover-the-park/towns-villages/balmaha/)

**Train access from the south** is via [Avanti West Coast](https://www.avantiwestcoast.co.uk/) into Glasgow, from stations including London (every 40 minutes, taking ~4½ hours), Birmingham (just over 4 hours) and Manchester (just over 3 hours).

**View from the Train** – Scottish Natural Heritage has a [free iPhone & Google Play (Android) app](https://www.nature.scot/enjoying-outdoors/places-visit/routes-explore/travelling-train) that provides an audio guide to a number of scenic train routes in Scotland including the route through the Park.

### By coach

There are two Citylink bus routes that cross the National Park:

- one of them going to Fort William/Skye from Glasgow has stops at Balloch, Duck Bay Beach, Luss, Inverbeg, Tarbet, Inveruglas, Ardlui, Inverarnan, Crianlarich and Tyndrum
- the other route going to Oban/Campbeltown also has stops at [Arrochar](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/discover-the-park/towns-villages/arrochar/), Ardgartan, Rest & Be Thankful and [Benmore Botanic Gardens](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/things-to-do/walking/hillwalking/benmore-botanic-gardens-viewpoint/)

See the [Citilink coach timetables](http://www.citylink.co.uk/timetables.php).

![silver-renault-car-parked-on-side-of-the-road-with-brown-hills-behind](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/05/Car-930x310-c-default.jpg)

Visiting by car

### By car

**From the south/east** – take the M74/M8 past Glasgow, then change to the M898 to the Erskine Bridge, then take the A82 into the National Park.

Drive times to [Balloch](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/discover-the-park/towns-villages/balloch/):

- Glasgow 35 minutes
- Edinburgh 90 minutes
- Manchester 4 hours
- Newcastle upon Tyne 3 hours 20 minutes
- Birmingham 5 hours 20 minutes
- London 7 hours 30 minutes

**From the north/west** – take the A82 into the National Park.

Drive times to [Balloch](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/discover-the-park/towns-villages/balloch/):

- Fort William 2 hours
- Inverness 3 hours 30 minutes
- Oban (A85 to A82) 1 hour 40 minutes

[Traffic Scotland](https://trafficscotland.org/) posts up-to-date traffic information.

If you’re driving an electric or plug-in hybrid vehicle, you can find a list of local charging points at [Zap Map](https://www.zap-map.com/).

### By airplane

- **[Glasgow Airport](https://www.glasgowairport.com/)** connects Scotland to the rest of the world, with direct flights to and from destinations across the globe
- Getting to Loch Lomond & The Trossachs National Park from the airport is pretty easy. All the major car rental brands are at the airport (near domestic arrivals). Once you have your car, getting to the National Park is simple. Follow the M8 west and then the M898 to the Erskine Bridge. Change to the A82 which will take you to [Balloch](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/discover-the-park/towns-villages/balloch/), the gateway to the Park and the west of [Loch Lomond](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/things-to-see/lochs-in-the-national-park/loch-lomond/)
- Likewise **[Edinburgh Airport](https://www.edinburghairport.com/)** has numerous international connections. The airport has a car rental centre with all the key hire brands. To get to Loch Lomond & The Trossachs National Park by public transport will require you to head to Glasgow first and change there
- **Seaplane** – [Loch Lomond](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/things-to-see/lochs-in-the-national-park/loch-lomond/) is home to the UK’s only [seaplane airline](https://www.lochlomondseaplanes.com/) and it provides aerial tours across the National Park and beyond

### By ferry

- [**Gourock – Dunoon** with Calmac Ferries](https://www.calmac.co.uk/article/7824/Dunoon-Gourock---Dunoon): regular ferries across to the Cowal Peninsula providing access to Argyll Forest.
- [**Gourock – Kilcreggan** with Calmac Ferries](https://www.calmac.co.uk/article/7824/Dunoon-Gourock---Dunoon); 15 minute crossing running approximately hourly, providing access to the Rosneath Peninsula and the National Park beyond.

The closest international ferry access for Scotland and the UK are at Stranraer (from Belfast), Newcastle (Holland), Hull (Belgium and Holland) and Liverpool (Dublin).

Find out more at [Traveline](https://www.travelinescotland.com/).

# Camping

# Go wild, or book a pitch

Camping is a great way to enjoy the National Park and there’s a wide choice of places to camp in stunning surroundings. You can choose from organised campsites around the National Park or alternatively, you can choose one of our lochshore permit areas. For those who prefer the solitude of ‘wild camping’ away from the hustle and bustle, there are plenty of places to immerse yourself in some of the most spectacular scenery in Scotland.

Whichever way you choose, please ensure you do it [**respectfully and responsibly**.](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/plan-your-visit/respect-park-stay-safe/camp-responsibly-ease-lockdown/) Here’s what you **[need to know before you go](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/things-to-do/camping/need-know-go/)**…

We are currently in the process of **[reviewing our Camping Management Byelaws](https://gbr01.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.lochlomond-trossachs.org%2Fpark-authority%2Fcamping-in-the-park-feedback-publications%2Fcamping-management-byelaws-review%2F&data=05%7C02%7CCathy.Owen%40lochlomond-trossachs.org%7Cd9611c47bd99486e868708de63dbb347%7C98d4a69a98cd498d88e2d652605ff305%7C0%7C0%7C639057992418313574%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=l5zm2F7aGTLl4LNwCec8iurHRLlZWzW9UsWrXhnaAWU%3D&reserved=0),** looking at how the Byelaws have worked in practice since they were introduced in 2017, and whether any changes are needed for the future. There will be a public consultation on findings from July – September 2026.

# Loch Lomond and The Trossachs National Park Loch Lomond and The Trossachs National Park National park in Scotland | Loch Lomond and The Trossachs National Park | | --- | | [IUCN category](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_protected_area_categories "IUCN protected area categories") V (protected landscape/seascape) | | [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/d/de/Loch_Katrine.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Loch_Katrine.jpg)
Looking eastwards along [Loch Katrine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Katrine "Loch Katrine") | | [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/72/Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park_UK_relief_location_map.png/960px-Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park_UK_relief_location_map.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park_UK_relief_location_map.png) | | Location | [Loch Lomond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond "Loch Lomond"), Scotland | | Coordinates | [56°15′N4°37′W﻿ / ﻿56.250°N 4.617°W﻿ / 56.250; -4.617](https://geohack.toolforge.org/geohack.php?pagename=Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park¶ms=56_15_N_4_37_W_type:landmark_dim:45km) | | Area | 1,865km2 (720sqmi)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park#cite_note-key-facts-1) | | Established | 2002 | | Governingbody | [National park authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_park_authority "National park authority") | | Website | [Official Website](https://www.lochlomond-trossachs.org/) | **Loch Lomond and The Trossachs National Park** ( [Scottish Gaelic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Gaelic_language "Scottish Gaelic language"): _Pàirc Nàiseanta Loch Laomainn is nan Tròisichean_) is a [national park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_park "National park") in [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland "Scotland") centred on [Loch Lomond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond "Loch Lomond") and the hills and glens of the [Trossachs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trossachs "Trossachs"), along with several other ranges of hills. It was the first of the [two national parks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_parks_of_Scotland "National parks of Scotland") established by the [Scottish Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_Parliament "Scottish Parliament") in 2002,[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park#cite_note-establish-2) the second being the [Cairngorms National Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cairngorms_National_Park "Cairngorms National Park"). The park extends to cover much of the western part of the southern [highlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highlands_of_Scotland "Highlands of Scotland"), lying to the north of the [Glasgow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glasgow "Glasgow") conurbation, and contains many mountains and lochs. It is the fourth-largest national park in the [British Isles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Isles "British Isles"), with a total area of 1,865km2 (720sqmi) and a boundary of some 350km (220mi) in length. It features 21 [Munros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munro "Munro") (including [Ben Lomond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Lomond "Ben Lomond"), [Ben Lui](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Lui "Ben Lui"), [Beinn Challuim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beinn_Challuim "Beinn Challuim"), [Ben More](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_More_(Crianlarich) "Ben More (Crianlarich)") and two peaks called [Ben Vorlich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Vorlich_(Loch_Lomond) "Ben Vorlich (Loch Lomond)")) and 20 [Corbetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hill_lists_in_the_British_Isles "Hill lists in the British Isles"). The park straddles the [Highland Boundary Fault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highland_Boundary_Fault "Highland Boundary Fault"), which divides it into two distinct regions - lowland and highland - that differ in underlying geology, soil types and topography.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park#cite_note-3) The change in rock type can most clearly be seen at Loch Lomond itself, as the fault runs across the islands of [Inchmurrin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inchmurrin "Inchmurrin"), [Creinch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Creinch "Creinch"), [Torrinch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torrinch "Torrinch") and [Inchcailloch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inchcailloch "Inchcailloch") and over the ridge of [Conic Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conic_Hill "Conic Hill"). To the south lie green fields and cultivated land; to the north, mountains.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park#cite_note-weir-4) The Loch Lomond and The Trossachs National Park lies close to Scotland's heavily populated [Central Belt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Belt "Central Belt"), and the area has long been popular with visitors. Principal attractions are viewing scenery and wildlife, walking, climbing, water sports, and other outdoor activities.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park#cite_note-5) In 2017, there were 2.9 million visits to the park, of which 2.1 million were day visits and 783,000 were made by visitors staying overnight within the park.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park#cite_note-visitors-6) ## Geography [![](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/31/Loch_Lomond_from_the_slopes_of_Ben_Lomond.jpg/500px-Loch_Lomond_from_the_slopes_of_Ben_Lomond.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Loch_Lomond_from_the_slopes_of_Ben_Lomond.jpg) Loch Lomond, viewed from the slopes of Ben Lomond. The national park extends to cover much of the western part of the southern [highlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highlands_of_Scotland "Highlands of Scotland"), lying to the north of the [Glasgow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glasgow "Glasgow") conurbation. The park authority defines the park as being split into four sections: [Breadalbane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breadalbane,_Scotland "Breadalbane, Scotland"), Loch Lomond, The Trossachs, and [Cowal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cowal "Cowal").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park#cite_note-areas-7) The park is centred on Loch Lomond, the largest lake in Great Britain by surface area,[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park#cite_note-8) with a surface area of 71km2 (27.5mi2).[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park#cite_note-weir-4) The loch contains many islands, including [Inchmurrin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inchmurrin "Inchmurrin"), the largest fresh-water island in the [British Isles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Isles "British Isles").[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park#cite_note-Worsley-9) It is a popular leisure destination, and is surrounded by hills,[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park#cite_note-theloch-10) including [Ben Lomond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Lomond "Ben Lomond") on the eastern shore, which is 973.7 metres (3,195ft) in height,[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park#cite_note-sheet56-11) and the most southerly of the Scottish [Munro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munro "Munro") peaks. A 2005 poll of _[Radio Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_Times "Radio Times")_ readers voted Loch Lomond as the sixth greatest natural wonder in Britain.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park#cite_note-12) The Trossachs are an area of wooded hills, glens and lochs that lie to the east of Loch Lomond. The name was originally applied only to a small woodland glen that lies at the centre of the area, but is now generally applied to the wider region. They have long been visited by tourists due to the relative proximity of major population centres such as [Glasgow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glasgow "Glasgow") and [Stirling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stirling "Stirling"), and the area remains popular with walkers, cyclists and tourists.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park#cite_note-SMC-13) The wooded hills and lochs of the area may be considered to represent a microcosm of a typical highland landscape,[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park#cite_note-SMC-13) and the woodlands are an important habitat for many species.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park#cite_note-qualities-14) Much of the Trossachs area is protected by various different [conservation designations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protected_areas_of_Scotland "Protected areas of Scotland"), including the "Great Trossachs Forest" [national nature reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_nature_reserve_(Scotland) "National nature reserve (Scotland)").[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park#cite_note-sitelink-15) Breadalbane refers to the northern part of the park, including the villages of [Crianlarich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crianlarich "Crianlarich") and [Tyndrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyndrum "Tyndrum"). The area consists of the steep hills and mountains of the southern highlands, and includes [Ben More](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_More_(Crianlarich) "Ben More (Crianlarich)"),[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park#cite_note-16) the highest mountain in the national park.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park#cite_note-key-facts-1) Breadalbane formed one of the [traditional provinces of Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provinces_of_Scotland "Provinces of Scotland"), and traditionally comprised the [watershed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drainage_divide "Drainage divide") of [Loch Tay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Tay "Loch Tay") (i.e. [Glen Dochart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glen_Dochart "Glen Dochart"), [Glen Lochay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glen_Lochay "Glen Lochay"), and the banks of Loch Tay itself), thus extending well beyond the boundaries of the national park.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park#cite_note-17)[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park#cite_note-18) The westernmost part of the park comprises the eastern side of the [Cowal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cowal "Cowal") peninsula, which is separated from the rest of the park by [Loch Long](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Long "Loch Long").[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park#cite_note-sheet56-11) Much of the peninsula is covered by the [Argyll Forest Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argyll_Forest_Park "Argyll Forest Park"), which is managed by [Forestry and Land Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forestry_and_Land_Scotland "Forestry and Land Scotland").[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park#cite_note-19) The [Arrochar Alps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrochar_Alps "Arrochar Alps"), a popular location for hillwalking and climbing, lie at the northern edge of Cowal, overlooking Loch Lomond.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park#cite_note-20) Several major transport routes pass through the park, including the [A82 road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A82_road "A82 road") between [Glasgow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glasgow "Glasgow") and [Fort William](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_William,_Highland "Fort William, Highland"), which follows the western shore of Loch Lomond, continuing north via [Strath Fillan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strath_Fillan "Strath Fillan") to bypass the village of [Crianlarich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crianlarich "Crianlarich") and pass through [Tyndrum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyndrum "Tyndrum"). The [A85 road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A85_road "A85 road") from [Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh "Edinburgh") passes to the east of the Trossachs and through the Breadalbane area of the park, meeting the A82 at Crianlarich. The only railway in the national park is the [West Highland Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Highland_Line "West Highland Line"), which follows the eastern shore of Loch Long as far as [Arrochar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arrochar,_Argyll_and_Bute "Arrochar, Argyll and Bute"), and thence runs close to the A82 as far as Tyndrum.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park#cite_note-sheet56-11)[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park#cite_note-sheet50-21) ## Formation of the national park Many countries have established national parks on the basis of setting aside areas of wilderness; Scotland however, lacks any such areas, as thousands of years of human activity have altered the landscape. Human settlement and activity, including [agriculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agriculture "Agriculture"), historical [deforestation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deforestation "Deforestation"), [overgrazing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overgrazing "Overgrazing") by [sheep](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheep "Sheep") and [deer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deer "Deer"), and extensive 20th century [afforestation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afforestation "Afforestation") with [introduced](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exotic_species "Exotic species") tree species (particularly [conifers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conifer "Conifer")) have resulted in landscapes which are best described as semi-natural.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park#cite_note-wildness-22) Despite the lack of true "wilderness" the idea that areas of Scotland having wild or remote character should be designated to protect the environment and encourage public access grew in popularity throughout the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Following the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), a committee was established to consider the issue of national parks in Scotland. The report, published in 1945, proposed national parks in five areas, one of which was Loch Lomond and The Trossachs.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loch_Lomond_and_The_Trossachs_National_Park#

# Be a responsible visitor

The National Park is a special place for everyone to respect, protect and enjoy. We all have a role to play in keeping it that way.

Being a responsible visitor starts before you even leave home. Plan ahead so you can make the most of your visit, avoid disappointment and minimise your impact on climate and nature.
